question: What temperature do I have to keep hot food at on the line or while it waits for a delivery driver?
reference_answer: At 57°C (135°F) or above; roasts cooked as in 3-401.11(B) may be held at 54°C (130°F) or above.

question: What temperature should our walk-in fridge keep prepared food at?
reference_answer: At 5°C (41°F) or less.

question: What internal temperature does chicken need to reach when we cook it?
reference_answer: 74°C (165°F) or above for less than 1 second (instantaneous).

question: What temperature do burgers made from ground beef have to be cooked to?
reference_answer: 68°C (155°F) for 17 seconds, or an equivalent from the chart: 63°C (145°F) for 3 minutes, 66°C (150°F) for 1 minute, 70°C (158°F) instantaneous.

question: We made chili yesterday and cooled it. What temperature do we have to reheat it to before putting it back in the hot-holding unit?
reference_answer: All parts to at least 74°C (165°F) for 15 seconds, done rapidly: no more than 2 hours between 5°C (41°F) and 74°C. In a microwave: 74°C, rotated or stirred, covered, and left to stand covered 2 minutes.

question: How many days can we keep a soup or sauce we made in the fridge before we have to throw it out?
reference_answer: At most 7 days at 5°C (41°F) or less, counting the day of preparation as Day 1; it must be date-marked if kept more than 24 hours.

question: One of our cooks wants to make desserts at home and bring them in to sell at the restaurant. Is that allowed?
reference_answer: No. Food prepared in a private home may not be used or offered for human consumption in a food establishment.

question: How long do staff need to wash their hands for?
reference_answer: At least 20 seconds in total, rubbing vigorously with soap for at least 10 to 15 seconds, then rinsing under clean, running warm water and drying.

question: Can our cooks wear a wedding ring while preparing food?
reference_answer: Yes. Jewelry on the arms and hands is not allowed while preparing food, except a plain ring such as a wedding band (and a medically necessary device for someone covered by the ADA).

question: Can staff plate salads or make sandwiches with their bare hands?
reference_answer: No. Exposed ready-to-eat food may not be touched with bare hands; use utensils such as deli tissue, spatulas, tongs, single-use gloves or dispensing equipment. Exceptions: when it is added to food that will be cooked, or with prior approval and written procedures (not when serving a highly susceptible population).

question: What are the approved ways to thaw frozen chicken?
reference_answer: Under refrigeration that keeps it at 5°C (41°F) or less; completely submerged under running water at 21°C (70°F) or below (with time limits); as part of cooking; or in a microwave and immediately moved to conventional cooking.

question: Which ingredients count as major food allergens?
reference_answer: Milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, wheat, peanuts, soybeans and sesame, and food ingredients containing protein from them (not highly refined oils made from them).

question: We serve burgers cooked to order, including rare. Do we have to warn customers?
reference_answer: Yes, with a consumer advisory: a disclosure (describe the item or asterisk it to a footnote) and a reminder footnote such as 'Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness', on the menu, placards, labels or other written means.

question: We package grab-and-go salads to sell. What has to be on the label?
reference_answer: The common name; the ingredients in descending order by weight (including artificial colors, flavors and chemical preservatives); net quantity; name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer or distributor; the food source of each major food allergen; and nutrition labeling unless exempt.

question: Does our manager on duty need a food safety certification?
reference_answer: Yes. The person in charge must be a certified food protection manager who passed a test from an accredited program, unless the regulatory authority considers the establishment minimal risk.

question: Can the owner's dog stay in the kitchen while we prep food?
reference_answer: No. Live animals may not be allowed on the premises of a food establishment; the exceptions (such as service animals in customer areas not used for food preparation) do not cover a pet in the kitchen.

question: How accurate do our food thermometers have to be?
reference_answer: Accurate to ±1°C if scaled in Celsius or in both Celsius and Fahrenheit, or to ±2°F if scaled only in Fahrenheit.

question: When we sanitize pans in the sink with hot water, how long do they need to stay in the water?
reference_answer: At least 30 seconds of immersion (hot water manual operations).

question: Can a cook use the same gloves to cut raw chicken and then make a salad?
reference_answer: No. Single-use gloves are used for only one task, such as working with raw animal food or with ready-to-eat food, and for no other purpose; they are discarded when damaged, soiled or when the work is interrupted.

question: A cook threw up this morning before her shift. When can she come back to work?
reference_answer: Not until at least 24 hours have passed after the vomiting (and any diarrhea) ended; she should phone the manager rather than come in.

question: Can staff use hand sanitizer instead of washing their hands?
reference_answer: No. Hand antiseptics may only be used in addition to proper handwashing.

question: What is the 'temperature danger zone'?
reference_answer: The range where pathogens grow fastest on TCS foods, usually between 41°F and 135°F (5°C and 57°C).

question: Do our cooks have to wear hairnets?
reference_answer: They must wear hair restraints such as hats, hair coverings or nets, beard restraints, and clothing that covers body hair, so hair cannot touch exposed food or clean equipment; not required for counter staff serving only drinks or wrapped food, hosts and wait staff with minimal risk.

question: Our soup cooled to 70°F after one hour. How much longer do we have to get it down to fridge temperature?
reference_answer: Cooked TCS food must be cooled from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours and to 5°C (41°F) or less within a total of 6 hours. Since it reached 70°F after 1 hour, 5 hours remain to reach 41°F (the guide: if 70°F is reached before 2 hours, you keep the remaining time).

question: We cook a big batch of rice every morning. How fast must it be cooled, and what methods can we use?
reference_answer: From 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within 2 hours and to 5°C (41°F) within a total of 6 hours. Methods: shallow pans, smaller or thinner portions, rapid cooling equipment, stirring in an ice water bath, containers that transfer heat, adding ice as an ingredient, a depth of no more than 2 inches; containers arranged for heat transfer and loosely covered.

question: We're thinking of opening a delivery-only kitchen. Does that count as a food establishment, and could we sell food that someone prepared at home?
reference_answer: Yes, it is a food establishment: the definition covers operations that hand food to consumers directly or through a delivery service such as takeout orders, and includes commissaries. Food prepared in a private home may not be used or offered in a food establishment.

question: We cook chicken thighs and keep them warm for takeout orders. What temperature do we cook them to, and what temperature do we hold them at?
reference_answer: Cook to 74°C (165°F) or above (instantaneous); then hold at 57°C (135°F) or above.

question: How warm does the water at our handwashing sink have to be?
reference_answer: The Food Code 2026 requires at least 29.4°C (85°F) through a mixing valve or combination faucet. The Handbook quotes the 2017 Food Code's 38°C (100°F), which is outdated.

question: A cook tells me his eyes have turned yellow. Do I have to send him home, and do I need to tell anyone?
reference_answer: Exclude him if the jaundice started within the last 7 days, unless a health practitioner documents it is not caused by hepatitis A or another fecal-orally transmitted infection. Report the jaundice to the regulatory authority, whose approval is needed before he returns.

question: We made potato salad on Monday and keep it at 41°F. What is the last day we can serve it, and what if someone forgot to put a date on it?
reference_answer: Monday counts as Day 1 and it may be kept at most 7 days, so through Sunday. Food that must be date-marked but whose container bears no date must be discarded.

question: A cook switches from cutting raw chicken to making salads. Is changing gloves enough?
reference_answer: No. The gloves must be changed because single-use gloves are for one task only, and the cook must also wash hands when switching between raw food and ready-to-eat food and before putting on new gloves.
